subChunks.title: EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, and Anti-join Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any rows at all — without caring what those rows contain. It is often clearer and faster than IN with a subquery.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
EXISTS

-- Apprentices who have at least one quest completion:
SELECT a.name
FROM   apprentices AS a
WHERE  EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM quest_completions AS qc
  WHERE qc.apprentice_id = a.id
);

The inner query uses SELECT 1 — the actual columns returned don't matter. EXISTS only asks: does this subquery return at least one row?

NOT EXISTS — the anti-join alternative

-- Apprentices who have completed NO quest:
SELECT a.name
FROM   apprentices AS a
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM quest_completions AS qc
  WHERE qc.apprentice_id = a.id
);

NOT EXISTS is the safest anti-join form — it handles NULLs correctly, unlike NOT IN (which silently returns zero rows if the subquery contains any NULLs).

EXISTS vs IN — key difference

-- NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM quest_completions);
-- If ANY row in quest_completions has NULL apprentice_id,
-- this returns ZERO rows (because x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) = UNKNOWN)

-- NOT EXISTS is safe:
SELECT name FROM apprentices AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM quest_completions qc WHERE qc.apprentice_id = a.id);
-- NULL rows in completions do not affect this result

storyBeats.text: 'Find all apprentices who have never been on a quest.' NOT IN feels natural — but Cipher shakes his head.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: NOT IN has a NULL trap. If any row in the subquery has a NULL apprentice_id — perhaps a quest logged without attribution — NOT IN returns nothing. Silently. NOT EXISTS is immune to NULLs. When finding rows that are absent from another table, always use NOT EXISTS.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN when the subquery might contain NULL values. Give a concrete example of the bug NOT IN causes.

options: Whether the subquery returns at least one row — the actual column values don't matter
Whether the subquery returns exactly one row
Whether all rows in the subquery match the outer condition
Whether the subquery column equals the outer column
questions.answer: Whether the subquery returns at least one row — the actual column values don't matter
questions.explanation: EXISTS is a boolean test: true if the subquery produces any rows, false if it produces none. That is why `SELECT 1` is commonly used inside — the value is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: A quest_completions table has one row with apprentice_id = NULL. What does `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM quest_completions)` return?
options: Zero rows — because x NOT IN (list with NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row
An error — NULL is not allowed in IN subqueries
The same result as NOT EXISTS
questions.answer: Zero rows — because x NOT IN (list with NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row
questions.explanation: x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is equivalent to x != 1 AND x != 2 AND x != NULL. x != NULL is always UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN AND anything = UNKNOWN. WHERE filters out UNKNOWN, so all rows disappear.

questions.prompt: Why is `SELECT 1` used inside EXISTS rather than `SELECT *`?
options: The actual values returned by the subquery are irrelevant — EXISTS only checks for row existence, and SELECT 1 makes the intent explicit
SELECT * is not allowed inside EXISTS
SELECT 1 is faster because it returns fewer bytes
questions.answer: The actual values returned by the subquery are irrelevant — EXISTS only checks for row existence, and SELECT 1 makes the intent explicit
questions.explanation: EXISTS ignores what the subquery returns — it only tests whether any row exists. SELECT 1 signals to readers that the values are irrelevant. SELECT * also works but SELECT 1 is the idiom.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN?
options: Always when the subquery column might contain NULLs — NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly; NOT IN does not
Only when the subquery returns more than 1000 rows
When you want an error if NULLs are present
NOT EXISTS and NOT IN are always equivalent
questions.answer: Always when the subquery column might contain NULLs — NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly; NOT IN does not
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS never has the NULL trap. It is the correct anti-join pattern whenever the subquery column is nullable. Even if the column is NOT NULL today, a schema change could introduce NULLs — using NOT EXISTS is defensively correct.
